label: q:main-inverse
title: Question
body_md:
\label{q:main-inverse}
If two graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ have cospectral transposition Cayley graphs
$\Gamma(G_1)$ and $\Gamma(G_2)$, must $G_1$ and $G_2$ be isomorphic?
More generally, which invariants of $G$ are determined by
$\operatorname{Spec}(\Gamma(G))$?
head: environment

label: prop:bipartite-symmetry
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:bipartite-symmetry}
For every graph $G$, the Cayley graph $\Gamma(G)$ is bipartite.  Its two
parts are the even and odd permutations in $S_n$.  Consequently its
adjacency spectrum is symmetric about zero, and
\[
 M_{2r+1}(G)=0
 \qquad (r\geq 0).
\]
head: environment
name: Bipartite symmetry

title: Proof
body_md:
Every generator in $T_G$ is a transposition, hence changes the parity of
a permutation.  Thus every edge of $\Gamma(G)$ joins an even permutation
to an odd permutation.  The spectral symmetry is the standard spectral
symmetry of a finite bipartite graph, and the vanishing of odd moments is
equivalent to the absence of closed walks of odd length.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
For every simple graph $G$ and every $k\geq 0$ one has
\[
 \frac{M_k(G)}{n!}
 =
 \sum_F c_k(F) N_F(G),
\]
where the sum is over all isomorphism classes of finite simple graphs
$F$ with no isolated vertices and with at most $k$ edges.
head: environment
name: Universal support expansion

title: Proof
body_md:
By the coefficient-of-the-identity formula,
\[
 \frac{M_k(G)}{n!}
 =
 \#\{(e_1,\ldots,e_k)\in E(G)^k:
      \tau_{e_1}\cdots\tau_{e_k}=1\}.
\]
To each such word associate its support, namely the subgraph of $G$
spanned by the distinct edges appearing among $e_1,\ldots,e_k$ and their
endpoints.  The support has no isolated vertices and at most $k$ edges.
For a fixed subgraph $H\subseteq G$ isomorphic to $F$, the number of
identity words of length $k$ whose support is exactly $H$ is precisely
$c_k(F)$, since the transposition relations depend only on the abstract
incidence pattern of $H$.  Summing over all possible supports gives the
formula.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The constants $c_k(F)$ are algorithmically computable.  For fixed $k$
there are only finitely many graphs $F$ with at most $k$ edges, and one
can enumerate all words of length $k$ in the edge-transpositions of $F$.
This gives a finite, completely explicit procedure for producing the
moment formula of any prescribed order.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The support expansion gives another way to see the parity phenomenon in
Proposition~\ref{prop:bipartite-symmetry}: $c_k(F)=0$ for every odd
$k$.  The first nontrivial moments are therefore $M_2,M_4,M_6,\ldots$.
head: environment

label: thm:rank-bound
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:rank-bound}
If $c_k(F)\neq 0$, then
\[
 2\operatorname{rk}(F)\le k
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad |E(F)|\le k .
\]
In particular a connected support of an identity word of length $k$ has
at most $k/2+1$ vertices.  Consequently
\[
 \frac{M_{2r}(G)}{n!}=
 \sum_{\substack{F:\ \operatorname{rk}(F)\le r\\ |E(F)|\le 2r}}
 c_{2r}(F)\,N_F(G).
\]
head: environment
name: Hurwitz-type rank bound

title: Proof
body_md:
The inequality $|E(F)|\le k$ is clear, since a word of length $k$ uses
at most $k$ distinct letters.  Let $(e_1,\dots,e_k)$ be a word counted
by $c_k(F)$.  Put $\sigma_0=1$ and $\sigma_j=\tau_{e_j}\sigma_{j-1}$, and
let $\operatorname{cyc}(\sigma)$ be the number of cycles of $\sigma$ on
$V(F)$, fixed points included.  Multiplying by a transposition $(ab)$
changes the number of cycles by $\pm1$.  It decreases by one exactly
when $a$ and $b$ lie in different cycles of the permutation being
multiplied.

Let $F_j$ be the graph on $V(F)$ with edges $e_1,\dots,e_j$.  The cycles
of $\sigma_{j-1}$ are contained in the orbits of the group generated by
$\tau_{e_1},\dots,\tau_{e_{j-1}}$, and these orbits are the connected
components of $F_{j-1}$.  Hence, whenever $e_j$ joins two different
components of $F_{j-1}$, the number of cycles drops by one at step $j$.
Passing from the edgeless graph $F_0$ to $F_k=F$ requires exactly
$|V(F)|-c(F)=\operatorname{rk}(F)$ such merging steps.  So at least
$\operatorname{rk}(F)$ steps decrease the number of cycles.  Since
$\sigma_k=\sigma_0=1$, the numbers of decreasing and increasing steps
are equal.  Therefore $k\ge 2\operatorname{rk}(F)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For a connected support $F$ on $v$ vertices the bound reads
$k\ge 2(v-1)$.  By the Riemann--Hurwitz formula, an identity word of
length $k$ generating a transitive subgroup corresponds to a branched
covering of the sphere by a surface of genus $g$ with
$k=2(v-1)+2g$.  The words with $k=2(v-1)$ are the \emph{minimal
transitive factorizations} of the identity.  Their total number in $S_n$
is a classical Hurwitz number; see Corollary~\ref{cor:hurwitz}.  Thus
the support expansion is naturally graded by genus, and the support
graphs $F$ refine the Hurwitz count according to which transpositions
are used.
head: environment

label: prop:exp-formula
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:exp-formula}
For a graph $F$ put
\[
 C_F(x)=\sum_{k\ge0}c_k(F)\frac{x^k}{k!}.
\]
If $F=F_1\sqcup F_2$ is a vertex-disjoint union, then
$C_F(x)=C_{F_1}(x)\,C_{F_2}(x)$, that is,
\[
 c_k(F_1\sqcup F_2)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj c_j(F_1)\,c_{k-j}(F_2).
\]
Moreover
\[
 \sum_{k\ge0}\frac{M_k(G)}{n!}\frac{x^k}{k!}
 =[1]\,e^{xA_G}
 =\sum_{F}C_F(x)\,N_F(G),
\]
where $F$ runs over all graphs without isolated vertices, the empty
graph included, with $C_\emptyset=1$.
head: environment
name: Exponential formula

title: Proof
body_md:
A word in $E(F_1)\sqcup E(F_2)$ is a shuffle of a word in $E(F_1)$ and a
word in $E(F_2)$, and there are $\binom kj$ ways to interleave words of
lengths $j$ and $k-j$.  The transpositions of $F_1$ commute with those
of $F_2$, and the corresponding subgroups intersect trivially.  So the
product is the identity if and only if both subwords have identity
product.  A word uses every edge of $F$ if and only if each subword uses
every edge of its own component.  The second statement is the
exponential generating function form of the support expansion.
head: environment

label: cor:hurwitz
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:hurwitz}
For every $n\ge 2$,
\[
 \sum_{\substack{F\subseteq K_n\\ F\ \text{spanning, connected}}}
 c_{2n-2}(F)=(2n-2)!\,n^{n-3},
\]
where the sum is over labelled spanning connected subgraphs of $K_n$.
Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{[F]}c_{2n-2}(F)\,\frac{n!}{|\operatorname{Aut}F|}=(2n-2)!\,n^{n-3},
\]
the sum running over isomorphism classes of connected graphs on $n$
vertices.
head: environment
name: Genus-zero Hurwitz numbers

title: Proof
body_md:
The left-hand side counts words of length $2n-2$ in the transpositions
of $S_n$ whose product is $1$ and which generate a transitive subgroup,
i.e.\ minimal transitive factorizations of the identity.  By Hurwitz's
formula (proved rigorously by Goulden and Jackson
\cite{Hurwitz,GouldenJackson97}), the number of minimal transitive
factorizations of a permutation of cycle type
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_\ell)\vdash n$ is
$(n+\ell-2)!\,n^{\ell-3}\prod_i\alpha_i^{\alpha_i}/(\alpha_i-1)!$.
For $\alpha=1^n$ this equals $(2n-2)!\,n^{n-3}$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
For every $k$, the same spectral invariant $M_k(G)$ admits both
expressions
\[
 \frac{M_k(G)}{n!}=\sum_F c_k(F)N_F(G)
\]
and
\[
 M_k(G)=
 \sum_{\lambda\vdash n} f^\lambda
 \operatorname{tr}\left(
 \left(\sum_{e\in E(G)}\rho_\lambda(\tau_e)\right)^k
 \right).
\]
The first expression organizes the answer by subgraph supports in $G$;
the second organizes it by irreducible representations of $S_n$.
head: environment
name: Two all-order descriptions

label: prop:standard-laplacian
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:standard-laplacian}
On the permutation representation $W=\mathbb C^n$ one has
\[
 \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}(ij)=mI-L_G.
\]
Consequently, on the standard representation $W_0$ the operator
$A_G^{(n-1,1)}$ has eigenvalues
\[
 m-\lambda_2,\,m-\lambda_3,\ldots,\,m-\lambda_n,
\]
where
\[
 0=\lambda_1\leq \lambda_2\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n
\]
are the Laplacian eigenvalues of $G$.
head: environment
name: The standard component

title: Proof
body_md:
For a single edge $\{i,j\}$, the transposition $(ij)$ fixes the
orthogonal complement of the line spanned by $e_i-e_j$ and sends
$e_i-e_j$ to its negative.  Therefore, as an operator on $W$,
\[
 (ij)=I-(e_i-e_j)(e_i-e_j)^t.
\]
Summing this identity over all edges gives
\[
 A_G=mI-\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}(e_i-e_j)(e_i-e_j)^t=mI-L_G.
\]
The vector $(1,\ldots,1)$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $m$, and the
restriction to its complement is exactly the standard representation.
This proves the assertion.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{prop:standard-laplacian} should be interpreted with a
minor caveat.  The full Cayley spectrum records the union of the spectra
of all irreducible components, with multiplicities, but it does not label
which eigenvalues come from which component.  Thus the proposition shows
that the \emph{refined} irreducible spectrum contains the Laplacian
spectrum of $G$.  It also explains why the transposition Cayley spectrum
is naturally expected to be stronger than the ordinary adjacency or
Laplacian spectrum: the latter appears already in the single component
$(n-1,1)$, while all other irreducible representations provide additional
constraints.
head: environment

label: thm:token
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:token}
On $M^{(n-k,k)}$ one has
\[
 mI-\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}(ij)=L_{F_k(G)},
\]
the Laplacian of the $k$-token graph.  Consequently, for $1\le k\le n/2$,
the multiset $m-\operatorname{Spec}A_G^{(n-k,k)}$ is the multiset
difference
\[
 \operatorname{LSpec}F_k(G)\setminus\operatorname{LSpec}F_{k-1}(G),
\]
where $\operatorname{LSpec}$ denotes the Laplacian spectrum.
head: environment
name: Token graphs

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $S$ be a $k$-subset and $e=\{i,j\}\in E(G)$.  If $e\subseteq S$ or
$e\cap S=\emptyset$, then $(ij)S=S$.  Otherwise
$(ij)S=S\triangle\{i,j\}$, which is a neighbour of $S$ in $F_k(G)$, and
every neighbour arises from exactly one edge.  Hence $A_G$ acts on
$M^{(n-k,k)}$ as $A(F_k(G))+D$, where $D$ is diagonal with entry
$m-\deg_{F_k(G)}(S)$ at $S$.  Thus $mI-A_G=L_{F_k(G)}$.  The second
statement follows by induction on $k$ from Young's rule.
head: environment

label: cor:aldous
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:aldous}
Let $G$ be connected, and let $a(G)=\lambda_2(L_G)$ be its algebraic
connectivity.  Then the largest eigenvalue of $\Gamma(G)$ other than $m$
is
\[
 \lambda_2(\Gamma(G))=m-a(G),
\]
and by bipartite symmetry the smallest eigenvalue other than $-m$ is
$-(m-a(G))$.  In particular $\operatorname{Spec}\Gamma(G)$ determines
$a(G)$.  Also, for every Laplacian eigenvalue $\mu\neq 0$ of $G$, the
number $m-\mu$ is an eigenvalue of $\Gamma(G)$ with multiplicity at
least $(n-1)\operatorname{mult}_{L_G}(\mu)$.
head: environment
name: The spectrum determines the algebraic connectivity

title: Proof
body_md:
The operator $mI-A_G$ on $\mathbb C[S_n]$ is the generator of the
interchange process on $G$ with unit rates, and $L_G$ is the generator
of the random walk on $G$.  The Caputo--Liggett--Richthammer theorem
\cite{CLR} (Aldous' spectral gap conjecture) says that their spectral
gaps coincide.  Since $G$ is connected, the eigenvalue $m$ of $\Gamma(G)$
is simple (Theorem~\ref{thm:connectedness-test}), so the spectral gap of
the interchange process is $m-\lambda_2(\Gamma(G))$.  This proves the
first statement.  The multiplicity bound follows from
Proposition~\ref{prop:standard-laplacian}, since $V_{(n-1,1)}$ occurs
$n-1$ times in the regular representation.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In the language of token graphs, Corollary~\ref{cor:aldous} says that
$a(F_k(G))=a(G)$ for all $k$.  Dalf\'o et al.\ conjectured this, and it
was later recognised to be a consequence of the
Caputo--Liggett--Richthammer theorem \cite{DalfoEtAl,DalfoFiol}.  We
checked $\lambda_2(\Gamma(G))=m-a(G)$ numerically for all
connected graphs with at most $8$ vertices.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
For every fixed $k$, the normalized moment $M_k(G)/n!$ belongs to the
finite-dimensional span of the subgraph-counting functions $N_F(G)$ with
at most $k$ edges.  In particular, for fixed $k$ it depends only on the
numbers of small subgraphs of $G$.
head: environment
name: Moments are finite-type graph invariants

title: Question
body_md:
Do the functions $M_2,M_4,\ldots,M_{2r}$ determine any natural triangular
system of subgraph-counting functions $N_F(G)$, at least after restricting
to graphs with a fixed number of vertices or to natural subclasses such
as triangle-free graphs?
head: environment

title: Question
body_md:
Do the even Cayley moments determine the power sums
\[
 \sum_{v\in V(G)} d_v^q
\]
of the degree sequence?  Equivalently, do they determine the degree
sequence of $G$?
head: environment

label: thm:weighted-fourth
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:weighted-fourth}
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph on $n$ vertices.  For every edge $e$,
\[
 [y_e^4]\,\mathcal R_4(G;\mathbf y)=n!,
\]
and for two distinct edges $e,f$,
\[
 [y_e^2y_f^2]\,\mathcal R_4(G;\mathbf y)=
 \begin{cases}
 4n!,& e\cap f\neq\varnothing,\\
 6n!,& e\cap f=\varnothing.
 \end{cases}
\]
Consequently the polynomial $\mathcal R_4(G;\mathbf y)$, considered up
to permutation of the edge variables, determines the line graph $L(G)$.
Moreover, among connected simple graphs it determines $G$ up to
isomorphism.
head: environment
name: Weighted fourth-trace reconstruction

title: Proof
body_md:
The coefficient of $y_e^4$ comes from the single word $eeee$, whose product
is the identity.  For $e\neq f$ there are six words containing two copies
of each letter.  If $e$ and $f$ are disjoint, the corresponding
transpositions commute, so all six words have identity product.  If they
are adjacent, four of the six words reduce by adjacent cancellations,
whereas the two alternating words $efef$ and $fefe$ are nontrivial because
$ef$ has order three.  This proves the coefficient formulae.

Hence the coefficient attached to each unordered pair of variables tells
whether the corresponding edges of $G$ meet, which is precisely the
adjacency relation in $L(G)$.  The pure fourth coefficient also recovers
$n!$, and hence $n$, whenever $G$ has an edge.  Whitney's line-graph theorem
\cite{Whitney} then reconstructs every connected simple graph, with the
only abstract line-graph ambiguity $K_3$ versus $K_{1,3}$ resolved by the
recovered value of $n$.  The connected edgeless case is just $K_1$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The theorem concerns a weighted refinement, not the ordinary Cayley
spectrum.  Setting every $y_e=1$ adds all pair coefficients together and
forgets which edge pairs are adjacent.  This is exactly why the unweighted
reconstruction problem remains nontrivial.  A parallel phenomenon occurs
in the $(n-2,2)$ component: \cite{ShapiroN22} shows that its weighted
quadratic trace already recovers $L(G)$ for $n\neq7$, while its weighted
quartic trace does so for every $n\ge4$.  Thus the same line-graph
mechanism appears both in the regular representation and in the first new
irreducible component, but at different trace degrees.
head: environment

label: thm:first-moments
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:first-moments}
Let $G$ be a simple graph.  Then
\[
\frac{M_0(G)}{n!}=1,
\qquad
\frac{M_1(G)}{n!}=0,
\qquad
\frac{M_2(G)}{n!}=N_{K_2}(G),
\qquad
\frac{M_3(G)}{n!}=0,
\]
\[
\frac{M_4(G)}{n!}
=
N_{K_2}(G)+4N_{P_3}(G)+6N_{2K_2}(G)+12N_{K_3}(G),
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{M_6(G)}{n!}
={}&N_{K_2}(G)
+20N_{P_3}(G)
+30N_{2K_2}(G)
+180N_{K_3}(G) \\
&+30N_{K_{1,3}}(G)
+42N_{P_4}(G)
+60N_{P_3\sqcup K_2}(G)
+90N_{3K_2}(G) \\
&+72N_{C_4}(G)
+96N_{\operatorname{Paw}}(G)
+180N_{K_3\sqcup K_2}(G) \\
&+132N_{K_4-e}(G)
+96N_{K_4}(G).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here all subgraph counts are non-induced.
head: environment
name: Moments up to order six

title: Proof
body_md:
The identities for $M_0$ and $M_1$ are immediate.  For $M_2$, a product
of two edge-transpositions is the identity if and only if the two
transpositions are equal.  Hence $M_2(G)/n!=N_{K_2}(G)$.

All odd moments vanish because a product of an odd number of
transpositions is an odd permutation and hence cannot be the identity.
This gives $M_3(G)=0$.

For $M_4$, the support of an identity word may have one, two, or three
edges.  If the support is a single edge, there is one word.  If the
support is a path $P_3$, i.e. two adjacent edges, there are four identity
words:
\[
aabb,
\quad abba,
\quad baab,
\quad bbaa.
\]
If the support is $2K_2$, i.e. two disjoint edges, the corresponding
transpositions commute, and all six words with two occurrences of each
edge are identity words.  Finally, if the support is a triangle with edge
transpositions $a,b,c$, then the Coxeter relation $aba=c$ and its cyclic
variants give twelve identity words of length four using all three
edges.  Equivalently, for every ordering of two adjacent triangle edges
one has a word of the form $abac=1$, and the same words are counted with
all cyclic choices of the distinguished edge.  This gives the displayed
fourth-moment formula.

The sixth moment is obtained from the universal support expansion by
enumerating the possible supports of length-six identity words.  There
are exactly thirteen support types with nonzero coefficient.  Their
coefficients $c_6(F)$ are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccccccc}
F & K_2 & P_3 & 2K_2 & K_3 & K_{1,3} & P_4 & P_3\sqcup K_2
& 3K_2 & C_4 & \operatorname{Paw} & K_3\sqcup K_2 & K_4-e & K_4 \\
\hline
c_6(F) & 1 & 20 & 30 & 180 & 30 & 42 & 60
& 90 & 72 & 96 & 180 & 132 & 96.
\end{array}
\]
Substituting these coefficients into
\[
\frac{M_6(G)}{n!}=\sum_F c_6(F)N_F(G)
\]
gives the formula.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The table in the proof was obtained by the following finite procedure.
For each support graph $F$ with at most six edges one enumerates all
$6$-tuples of edges of $F$ which use every edge of $F$ and multiplies the
corresponding transpositions in $S_{V(F)}$.  The displayed coefficient is
the number of such words with product equal to the identity.  This also
provides a short independent way to reproduce the formula and to compute
higher moments.  In the present version, all coefficients were
recomputed by machine.  We computed $c_k(F)$ for connected $F$ by
inclusion--exclusion over edge subsets, $c_k(F)=\sum_{H\subseteq
E(F)}(-1)^{|E(F)\setminus H|}W_k(H)$, where $W_k(H)$ is the number of
identity words of length $k$ over $H$, obtained by dynamic programming on
$S_{V(F)}$.  The disconnected coefficients then follow from
Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-formula}.  For example
$c_6(P_3\sqcup K_2)=\binom64\cdot4\cdot1=60$ and
$c_6(3K_2)=6!/2^3=90$.  All entries of the table were confirmed.  We
also checked $M_k(G)/n!=W_k(E(G))$ directly against the full regular
spectrum for random graphs with $n\le5$.
head: environment
name: Check of the enumeration

label: cor:fourth-moment-invariant
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:fourth-moment-invariant}
The Cayley spectrum of $\Gamma(G)$ determines
\[
 |E(G)|
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 6N_{K_3}(G)-N_{P_3}(G).
\]
In particular, on the class of triangle-free graphs it determines
$N_{P_3}(G)$ and therefore
\[
 \sum_{v\in V(G)}d_v^2.
\]
head: environment
name: The fourth-moment invariant

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $m=|E(G)|$, $P=N_{P_3}(G)$, $D=N_{2K_2}(G)$, and
$T=N_{K_3}(G)$.  The number $m$ is determined by $M_2(G)$.  Also
\[
D=\binom m2-P,
\]
because every unordered pair of distinct edges is either adjacent, hence
contributes to $P$, or disjoint, hence contributes to $D$.  Substituting
this into the fourth-moment formula gives
\[
 \frac{M_4(G)}{n!}
 =m+6\binom m2-2P+12T.
\]
Thus $6T-P$ is determined by the spectrum.  If $G$ is triangle-free, then
$T=0$, so $P$ is determined.  Finally,
\[
 P=\sum_{v\in V(G)}\binom{d_v}{2}
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \sum_v d_v^2=2P+2m.
\]
head: environment

label: cor:triangle-free-sixth
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:triangle-free-sixth}
Let $G$ be triangle-free.  Then the Cayley spectrum of $\Gamma(G)$
determines the linear combination
\[
 5N_{K_{1,3}}(G)+2N_{P_4}(G)+12N_{C_4}(G).
\]
If $G$ has girth at least five, this reduces to the determination of
\[
 5N_{K_{1,3}}(G)+2N_{P_4}(G).
\]
If, in addition, the maximum degree of $G$ is at most two, then the
spectrum determines $N_{P_4}(G)$.
head: environment
name: Triangle-free sixth-moment consequence

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $G$ is triangle-free and write
\[
 m=N_{K_2}(G),\quad P=N_{P_3}(G),\quad
 S=N_{K_{1,3}}(G),\quad R=N_{P_4}(G),\quad C=N_{C_4}(G).
\]
The disconnected support counts appearing in the sixth moment can be
eliminated in terms of these quantities.  First
\[
 N_{2K_2}=\binom m2-P.
\]
Next,
\[
 N_{P_3\sqcup K_2}=(m-2)P-3S-2R.
\]
Indeed, for each two-edge path $u-v-w$, the number of edges disjoint
from its three vertices is $m-d_u-d_v-d_w+2$; summing this over all
$P_3$'s and using triangle-freeness gives
\[
 \sum_{u-v-w}(d_u+d_v+d_w)=3S+4P+2R.
\]
Finally, classifying unordered triples of edges by their support gives
\[
 N_{3K_2}=\binom m3-N_{P_3\sqcup K_2}-S-R.
\]
Substitution into Theorem~\ref{thm:first-moments}, with all triangle
support types removed, yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{M_6(G)}{n!}
={}&m+30\binom m2+90\binom m3+(50-30m)P  \\
&+30S+12R+72C.
\end{aligned}
\]
By Corollary~\ref{cor:fourth-moment-invariant}, $m$ and $P$ are already
determined on the triangle-free class.  Hence $30S+12R+72C$, equivalently
$5S+2R+12C$, is determined.  The two stated specializations follow by
putting $C=0$ and then $S=0$.
head: environment

label: cor:regular-graphs
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:regular-graphs}
Let $G$ be a $d$-regular graph on $n$ vertices.  Then the Cayley spectrum
of $\Gamma(G)$ determines the number of triangles $N_{K_3}(G)$.  It also
determines the combination
\[
 6N_{C_4}(G)+11N_{K_4-e}(G)+8N_{K_4}(G).
\]
In particular, if $G$ is triangle-free and regular, then the Cayley
spectrum determines $N_{C_4}(G)$.  Hence this holds, in particular, for
regular bipartite graphs.
head: environment
name: Regular graphs: triangles and four-vertex supports

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $m=nd/2$ and $T=N_{K_3}(G)$.  Since
\[
 N_{P_3}(G)=n\binom d2,
\]
Corollary~\ref{cor:fourth-moment-invariant} immediately determines $T$;
more explicitly,
\[
 T=\frac1{12}\left(
 \frac{M_4(G)}{n!}-m-6\binom m2+2n\binom d2
 \right).
\]
We now use the sixth-moment formula.  In a regular graph the remaining
three-edge support counts are determined by $n,d,T$.  Indeed, putting
\[
 P=n\binom d2,\qquad S=n\binom d3,
\]
one has
\[
 N_{P_4}(G)=m(d-1)^2-3T,
\]
because a three-edge path is obtained by choosing its middle edge and one
further incident edge at each endpoint, except when the two new endpoints
coincide and form a triangle.  Counting adjacent edge-pairs inside an
unordered triple of edges gives
\[
 N_{P_3\sqcup K_2}(G)
 =(m-2)P-3T-3S-2N_{P_4}(G),
\]
and therefore
\[
 N_{3K_2}(G)=\binom m3-T-S-N_{P_4}(G)
              -N_{P_3\sqcup K_2}(G).
\]
The triangle-containing four-edge supports which occur in $M_6$ are also
fixed:
\[
 N_{\operatorname{Paw}}(G)=3(d-2)T,
 \qquad
 N_{K_3\sqcup K_2}(G)=(m-3d+3)T.
\]
After these quantities are substituted in Theorem~\ref{thm:first-moments},
the only undetermined terms are
\[
 72N_{C_4}(G)+132N_{K_4-e}(G)+96N_{K_4}(G).
\]
Thus the displayed combination after division by $12$ is determined by the
Cayley spectrum.  If $G$ is triangle-free then both $K_4-e$ and $K_4$ are
absent, so $N_{C_4}(G)$ is determined.
head: environment

label: thm:eighth
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:eighth}
For every graph $G$,
\[
 \frac{M_8(G)}{n!}=\sum_F c_8(F)\,N_F(G),
\]
where the nonzero coefficients are as follows.  For connected $F$ with at
most four vertices:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
F & K_2 & P_3 & K_3 & K_{1,3} & P_4 & \mathrm{Paw} & C_4 & K_4-e & K_4\\\hline
c_8(F) & 1 & 84 & 1932 & 420 & 552 & 3096 & 2832 & 10032 & 16896
\end{array}
\]
For connected $F$ on five vertices (these all satisfy
$k=8=2(|V(F)|-1)$, i.e.\ they are of genus zero):
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc|ccccc}
F & K_{1,4} & \mathrm{Ch} & P_5 & C_5 & \mathrm{Ban} & \mathrm{Bull} & \mathrm{Cr} & T_{3,2}\\\hline
c_8(F) & 336 & 608 & 816 & 400 & 1008 & 1448 & 1136 & 1952
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc|cccc|cc}
F & K_{2,3} & \mathrm{Ho} & \mathrm{Bf} & D_3 & D_2 & K_{1,1,3} & \mathrm{Gem} & K_4^{+} & W_4^- & K_5-P_3 & W_4\\\hline
c_8(F) & 1200 & 1536 & 3712 & 1584 & 2112 & 1920 & 1856 & 1248 & 1344 & 960 & 752
\end{array}
\]
For $K_5-e$ and $K_5$ the coefficient vanishes, since they have more than
eight edges.  For disconnected $F$, Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-formula}
gives the sixteen nonzero values
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
F & 2K_2 & 3K_2 & 4K_2 & P_3\sqcup 2K_2 & K_3\sqcup 2K_2 & P_3\sqcup K_2 & K_3\sqcup K_2 & K_{1,3}\sqcup K_2\\\hline
c_8(F) & 126 & 1260 & 2520 & 1680 & 5040 & 840 & 5880 & 840
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
F & P_4\sqcup K_2 & \mathrm{Paw}\sqcup K_2 & C_4\sqcup K_2 & (K_4-e)\sqcup K_2 & K_4\sqcup K_2 & 2P_3 & P_3\sqcup K_3 & 2K_3\\\hline
c_8(F) & 1176 & 2688 & 2016 & 3696 & 2688 & 1120 & 3360 & 10080
\end{array}
\]
head: environment
name: Eighth moment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-bound} and Proposition~\ref{prop:exp-formula},
it suffices to know $c_j(F)$ for $j\le 8$ and connected $F$ with at most
five vertices.  These were computed by the procedure described in the
remark following Theorem~\ref{thm:first-moments}.  As consistency
checks: the five-vertex coefficients, weighted by $5!/|\operatorname{Aut}F|$,
add up to the Hurwitz number $8!\cdot 5^2=1\,008\,000$ of
Corollary~\ref{cor:hurwitz}; summing $c_8$ over all edge subsets of random
graphs with $5\le n\le 7$ reproduces the exact number of identity words
of length $8$; and the values $c_4,c_6$ from the same computation reproduce
Theorem~\ref{thm:first-moments}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The same computation in length $10$ gives, for connected
graphs on six vertices,
\[
 c_{10}(K_{1,5})=5040,\qquad c_{10}(P_6)=25520,\qquad c_{10}(C_6)=2100,
\]
and the values of $c_{2e}(T)$ for the trees $T$ with $e\le 5$ edges are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
T & K_2&P_3&K_{1,3}&P_4&K_{1,4}&\mathrm{Ch}&P_5 \\\hline
c_{2e}(T)&1&4&30&42&336&608&816
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
T & K_{1,5} & S_{4} & DS & S(3,1,1) & S(2,2,1) & P_6\\\hline
c_{10}(T)& 5040 & 11220 & 14480 & 18880 & 19680 & 25520
\end{array}
\]
Here $S_4$ is $K_{1,4}$ with one edge subdivided, $DS$ is the double
star with degree sequence $(3,3,1,1,1,1)$, and $S(a,b,c)$ is the spider
with legs of lengths $a,b,c$.
head: environment

label: conj:closed
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:closed}
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For stars, $c_{2e}(K_{1,e})=\dfrac{(2e)!}{(e+1)!}=e!\,\mathrm{Cat}_e$.
\item For cycles, $c_{2(v-1)}(C_v)=v(v-1)^2\,\mathrm{Cat}_{v-2}$.
\item For a tree $T$, a word of length $2|E(T)|$ in the edges of $T$
using every edge has product $1$ if and only if every edge occurs exactly
twice and, for every vertex $x$ of $T$, the subword formed by the edges
incident to $x$ is a non-crossing double occurrence word.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Genus-zero closed formulae

title: Remark
body_md:
The correction term $12N_{K_3}(G)$ in the fourth moment is important.
It reflects the relation $(ij)(jk)(ij)=(ik)$ inside a triangle.  Thus
triangle effects begin at order four, not order six.  The sixth moment is
still the first place where the next family of local supports, such as
claws, four-vertex paths and four-cycles, enters the regular trace in a
substantial way.
head: environment

label: prop:complete-graph-spectrum
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:complete-graph-spectrum}
For $G=K_n$, the eigenvalue of $A_G=C_n$ on the irreducible
representation $V_\lambda$ is
\[
 \kappa_\lambda
 =
 \sum_{(a,b)\in\lambda}(b-a),
\]
the sum of the contents of all boxes of the Young diagram $\lambda$.
Equivalently,
\[
 \kappa_\lambda
 =
 \frac12\sum_i \lambda_i(\lambda_i-2i+1).
\]
In the regular representation this eigenvalue occurs with multiplicity
$(f^\lambda)^2$.
head: environment
name: Complete transposition graph

title: Proof
body_md:
The element $C_n$ is central.  Its scalar on $V_\lambda$ is the usual
central character of the transposition class.  In the Young--Jucys--
Murphy realization one has
\[
 C_n=J_2+J_3+\cdots+J_n,
 \qquad
 J_r=\sum_{i<r}(ir).
\]
The element $J_r$ acts diagonally in the Young orthogonal basis, with
eigenvalue equal to the content of the box containing $r$.  Summing over
$r$ gives the sum of all contents of $\lambda$.  The multiplicity
$(f^\lambda)^2$ follows from the decomposition of the regular
representation.
head: environment

label: prop:matching-spectrum
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:matching-spectrum}
If $G=mK_2$ is a matching with $m$ edges on $n$ vertices, then
\[
 \operatorname{Spec}(\Gamma(G))
 =
 \left\{\,m-2r:\;0\leq r\leq m\,\right\},
\]
where the eigenvalue $m-2r$ occurs with multiplicity
\[
 n!\,2^{-m}\binom mr.
\]
head: environment
name: Matching case

title: Proof
body_md:
The subgroup generated by the $m$ disjoint transpositions is
$(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^m$.  In a simultaneous eigenbasis for these
commuting involutions, each transposition contributes an eigenvalue
$\pm1$.  If exactly $r$ of the signs are negative, the sum is $m-2r$,
and there are $\binom mr$ such sign choices.  Each character of this
elementary abelian subgroup occurs in the regular representation of
$S_n$ with multiplicity $n!/2^m$.
head: environment

label: thm:star-spectrum
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:star-spectrum}
Let $G=K_{1,n-1}$.  Then the eigenvalues of $A_G$ are the possible
contents
\[
 c(b)=\operatorname{column}(b)-\operatorname{row}(b)
\]
of removable boxes $b$ of Young diagrams $\lambda\vdash n$.
More precisely, in the copy of $V_\lambda$ with Young orthogonal basis,
$A_G$ is diagonal and the basis vector indexed by a standard tableau $T$
has eigenvalue equal to the content of the box occupied by $n$ in $T$.
Thus the multiplicity of an integer $c$ in the regular representation is
\[
 \sum_{\lambda\vdash n}
 f^\lambda\,
 \#\{\,T\in \operatorname{SYT}(\lambda):
      c(\operatorname{box}_T(n))=c\,\}.
\]
head: environment
name: Star spectrum

title: Proof
body_md:
After choosing the centre of the star to be $n$, the operator $A_G$ is
exactly the Young--Jucys--Murphy element $J_n=\sum_{i<n}(in)$.  The
Young--Jucys--Murphy elements are diagonal in the Young orthogonal basis,
and $J_n$ acts on a standard tableau $T$ by the content of the box
containing $n$.  The stated multiplicity again follows by multiplying
the multiplicity inside $V_\lambda$ by the multiplicity $f^\lambda$ of
$V_\lambda$ in the regular representation.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The star theorem gives a genuine solution of one nontrivial instance of
the inverse problem.  Among stars, the Cayley spectrum determines the
number of leaves, hence the graph.  It also shows why the present
problem is naturally related to the Gelfand--Tsetlin and
Young--Jucys--Murphy approach to the representation theory of symmetric
groups.
head: environment

label: cor:solved-families
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:solved-families}
The reconstruction problem has an affirmative answer inside each of the
following families:
\[
 \{K_n\}_{n\geq1},\qquad
 \{mK_2\}_{m\geq0},\qquad
 \{K_{1,n-1}\}_{n\geq1}.
\]
In each case the transposition Cayley spectrum determines the parameter
of the family and hence the graph.
head: environment
name: A solved family of reconstruction examples

label: conj:reconstruction
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:reconstruction}
If
\[
\operatorname{Spec}(\Gamma(G_1))
=
\operatorname{Spec}(\Gamma(G_2)),
\]
then
\[
G_1\cong G_2.
\]
head: environment
name: Reconstruction conjecture

label: thm:connectedness-test
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:connectedness-test}
Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices with connected components of sizes
\[
 s_1,\ldots,s_r.
\]
Let $m=|E(G)|$.  Then the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $m$ in the
spectrum of $\Gamma(G)$ is
\[
 \frac{n!}{s_1!s_2!\cdots s_r!}.
\]
Consequently the spectrum of $\Gamma(G)$ determines whether $G$ is
connected.
head: environment
name: Connectedness test

title: Proof
body_md:
The Cayley graph $\Gamma(G)$ is $m$-regular.  For a finite undirected
$m$-regular graph, the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $m$ is equal to the
number of connected components of that graph.  The connected components
of a Cayley graph are the left cosets of the subgroup generated by its
connection set.  In the present case this subgroup is generated by all
transpositions corresponding to edges of $G$.

If $C_1,\ldots,C_r$ are the connected components of $G$, then the edge
transpositions generate
\[
 S_{C_1}\times S_{C_2}\times\cdots\times S_{C_r}
 \subseteq S_n,
\]
because transpositions along the edges of a connected graph generate the
full symmetric group on its vertex set.  Therefore the number of connected
components of $\Gamma(G)$ is the index
\[
 [S_n:S_{C_1}\times\cdots\times S_{C_r}]
 =\frac{n!}{s_1!s_2!\cdots s_r!}.
\]
In particular this multiplicity is equal to $1$ if and only if $r=1$,
which is exactly the connectedness of $G$.
head: environment

label: cor:necessary-conditions
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:necessary-conditions}
If $\Gamma(G_1)$ and $\Gamma(G_2)$ are cospectral, then $G_1$ and $G_2$
have the same number of vertices, the same number of edges, the same
value of $6N_{K_3}-N_{P_3}$, and the same value of
\[
 \prod_C |C|!,
\]
where the product is over the connected components $C$ of the graph.  In
particular, either both $G_1,G_2$ are connected or neither is connected.
If they are connected, they also have the same algebraic connectivity
$a(G_1)=a(G_2)$, by Corollary~\ref{cor:aldous}.
head: environment
name: Necessary conditions for Cayley cospectrality

title: Proof
body_md:
The number of vertices is determined by the size $n!$ of the Cayley
matrix, hence by the total multiplicity of the spectrum.  The number of
edges and the invariant $6N_{K_3}-N_{P_3}$ are determined by
Corollary~\ref{cor:fourth-moment-invariant}.  The product of factorials of
component sizes is determined from Theorem~\ref{thm:connectedness-test},
since the multiplicity of the top eigenvalue is
$n!/\prod_C |C|!$.
head: environment

label: thm:computer
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:computer}
\textup{(Computer-assisted.)}  For $n\le 9$, non-isomorphic graphs on
$n$ vertices have distinct moment vectors $(M_2,M_4,\dots,M_{10})$.  In
particular their transposition Cayley graphs are not cospectral, which
confirms Conjecture~\ref{conj:reconstruction} for $n\le 9$.  The minimal
number of even moments needed is $3$ for $n=5,6$, $4$ for $n=7$, and $5$
for $n=8,9$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For each graph we computed the refined spectrum numerically and the
normalized moments $M_{2j}(G)/n!$, which are integers.  For $j\le4$ the
floating-point values were within $10^{-7}$ of integers, so the
partition into classes by $(M_2,\dots,M_8)$ is exact.  For $n=8$ this
leaves five pairs of graphs, and for $n=7$ the classes of
$(M_2,M_4,M_6)$ leave $21$ classes.  In each such case we computed the
next moment \emph{exactly}, as the number $W_{2j}(E(G))$ of identity
words, by integer dynamic programming on $S_n$, and found that it
separates the graphs.

For $n=9$ the normalized moments of dense graphs are too large (of order
$36^{10}$) for exact rounding of floating-point values.  We therefore
regarded two graphs as possibly equal in $M_{2j}$ when the computed
values agreed to relative precision $10^{-10}$.  The numerical error is
of order $10^{-12}$, so graphs that differ at this precision are
certainly different.  Exactly $26$ pairs of graphs agree in
$M_2,\dots,M_8$ at this precision, and no two graphs agree in
$M_2,\dots,M_{10}$.  For each of the $26$ pairs we computed $W_8$ and
$W_{10}$ exactly on $S_9$: in every pair $W_8$ coincides and $W_{10}$
differs.  The graphs were generated by \texttt{geng}, so the list is
complete.
head: environment
name: Method

label: prop:counterexamples
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:counterexamples}
The moments $M_2,M_4,M_6$ do not determine the number of triangles, the
degree sequence, or the connectedness of $G$.  The moments
$M_2,M_4,M_6,M_8$ do not determine the number of triangles or the
degree sequence.  Explicitly, (a) and (b) are on the vertex set $[7]$,
and (c) is on $[9]$:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item $G_1=\{15,16,17,26,27,36,37,46,47,57,67\}$ and
$G_2=\{14,16,17,25,26,27,35,37,46,47,57\}$ are connected, with
$M_{2j}/7!=11,337,15837$ for $j=1,2,3$ for both.  However
$N_{K_3}(G_1)=5\neq4=N_{K_3}(G_2)$, and the degree sequences are
$(6,5,3,2,2,2,2)$ and $(5,3,3,3,3,3,2)$.  Their eighth moments are
$948029$ and $958353$.
\item $G_3=\{15,17,26,27,36,37,46,67\}$ is connected, and
$G_4=\{15,16,25,27,36,37,57,67\}$ is not (vertex $4$ is isolated).  Both
have $M_{2j}/7!=8,170,5186$ for $j=1,2,3$ and two triangles.  Their
eighth moments are $191786$ and $192546$.
\item The graphs
\[
\begin{aligned}
G_5&=\{16,17,19,26,28,29,37,38,39,48,49,59,69,79\},\\
G_6&=\{15,17,26,27,28,36,38,39,48,49,59,67,69,79\}
\end{aligned}
\]
are connected, with
$M_{2j}/9!=14,528,30010,2176660$ for $j=1,2,3,4$ for both.  However
$N_{K_3}(G_5)=4\neq3=N_{K_3}(G_6)$, and the degree sequences are
$(7,3,3,3,3,3,3,2,1)$ and $(5,4,4,3,3,3,2,2,2)$.  Their tenth moments
are $186799374$ and $187065334$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Limits of the low moments

title: Proof
body_md:
Direct computation of the numbers of identity words by integer dynamic
programming on $S_n$.  The values agree with those obtained from the
numerically computed refined spectra.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For $n=8$ there are exactly five pairs of non-isomorphic graphs with
equal $M_2,M_4,M_6,M_8$, and for $n=9$ there are exactly $26$ such pairs,
all connected.  For $n=8$, in all five pairs the two graphs have the same
degree sequence and the same number of triangles.  For $n=9$ this holds
for $23$ of the $26$ pairs; the exceptions include pair~(c) above.  For $n=8$, four of the five
pairs are Laplacian cospectral, so they also have the same
$(n-1,1)$-component of the refined spectrum.  None of them is adjacency
cospectral.  An example is the pair of triangle-free graphs
\[
\{15,17,18,25,27,28,36,37,38,46,47,48\},\quad
\{15,16,17,18,25,28,36,37,38,46,47,48\},
\]
with $M_{10}/8!=60025212$ and $60306492$ respectively.  Thus $M_2,\dots,M_8$ determine the number of triangles and the degree
sequence for $n\le 8$, but not for $n=9$.
head: environment
name: Pairs agreeing up to $M_8$

title: Question
body_md:
Is the number of triangles $N_{K_3}(G)$ determined by the full Cayley
spectrum of $\Gamma(G)$?  More modestly, is it determined by finitely
many even moments $M_2,M_4,\ldots,M_{2r}$?  By
Proposition~\ref{prop:counterexamples}(c), $r=4$ is not enough.
head: environment
name: Triangle problem

label: conj:degree
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:degree}
For each $q\geq 1$, the Cayley spectrum determines the power sum
\[
 p_q(G)=\sum_{v\in V(G)}d_v^q.
\]
Consequently, the Cayley spectrum determines the degree sequence of
$G$.
head: environment
name: Degree-power conjecture

title: Question
body_md:
Does the refined irreducible spectrum reconstruct $G$?  If not, does it
at least reconstruct all subgraph counts of $G$?
head: environment
